clue.text: Firebrands stirred up maturer blokes

indicators.note: stirring things up mixes them, so the letters of the two words are jumbled together

explanation.surface: Agitators have whipped up a crowd of older men.
explanation.definitionFit: Firebrands are agitators who stir up unrest, people who cause bother deliberately.

clue.text: Reprimands French perhaps helping in a big way

parts.note: French is an example of a tongue, a language
lashings is British informal for generous quantities, a big helping of food

explanation.surface: Someone is told off for heaping French food onto plates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lashings' is British slang for plenty, as in lashings of cream.
explanation.definitionFit: A severe scolding is a reprimand, so plural scoldings match plural reprimands.

clue.text: Start working at Pinewood?

definitions.meaning: Pinewood is a famous British film studio, so working there is being on the film set

explanation.walkthrough: Pinewood Studios, west of London, is where many British films are shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Onset is the beginning of something, as with the onset of winter.

clue.text: Inauspicious occasion when one has a terrible shock

definitions.meaning: a day when everything goes wrong

definitions.text: when one has a terrible shock
definitions.meaning: a shock is also a thick mass of hair, so a terrible shock is unruly hair

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shock' reads as a fright, but here it is a shock of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a day of frustration and misfortune, originally one when your hair will not behave.

clue.text: Pen love letters in order to cover up

indicators.note: the letters of the two words are put into a new order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone writes love letters neatly arranged so as to hide something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love letters' looks like a single phrase, but 'letters in order' is the signal to rearrange PEN LOVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To envelop something is to wrap it up completely, covering it over.

clue.text: Spot sailors taking ship round church

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor, so ABS are sailors
CE is the Church of England
SS is steamship

explanation.surface: Sailors are spotted taking their vessel around a church.
explanation.definitionFit: A spot or boil on the skin can be a pus-filled swelling of this kind.

clue.text: Eat out and so on with husband

parts.note: etc, et cetera, means and so on

explanation.surface: A couple dine out at restaurants and so forth with the husband.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eat out' suggests a restaurant, but it means to corrode, as acid does to metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Acid etches a plate by eating away its surface, so to engrave is to eat out.

clue.text: Modern sculptor's turning up collecting junk somewhere in palace

indicators.note: the sculptor's name collects junk, taking it in
in a down clue, turning up means the letters are read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: Henry Moore was a twentieth-century modern sculptor; with the 's he gives MOORES
tat is British slang for cheap junk

explanation.surface: A contemporary sculptor's work turns up in a palace, gathering rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning up' reads the whole assembly backwards, as befits a down entry. 'Modern' tempts toward Tate Modern, but it only describes Henry Moore; tat is British slang for junk.
explanation.definitionFit: A stateroom is a grand room for formal occasions, found in a palace or stately home.

clue.text: Whipped chocolate drunk all day long

indicators.note: whipping beats things up, so the letters are beaten into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Whipped chocolate drinks are consumed constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means continuously, day and night without stopping.

clue.text: Goes down fast with a lack of calming drugs, not having a temperature

indicators.note: the phrase does without the letters given by the following words

parts.note: no sedatives means a lack of tranquillisers
A plus T, the abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: A patient collapses quickly without tranquillisers and is free of fever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not having' removes A and T from NO SEDATIVES.
explanation.definitionFit: A nosedive is a steep, rapid fall, as with a plane or share prices plunging.

clue.text: One stuffing daily post in university

indicators.note: one goes into the other as stuffing goes into a bird

parts.note: a daily or char is a British term for a cleaning lady
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone stuffs the daily mail into a university pigeonhole.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'daily' is a British cleaner who comes in each day, also called a char.
explanation.definitionFit: A university chair is a professorship, a senior academic post.

clue.text: Extremist caught in awful tragedy

indicators.note: the letters are trapped inside the run of the two words

explanation.surface: A fanatic is arrested over a dreadful disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: An ultra is someone with extreme views, a hardliner or zealot.

clue.text: Release unauthorised information on radio — one of five a day?

indicators.note: on the radio things are heard, not seen, so the word is given by its sound

parts.note: to leak is to pass on secrets

explanation.surface: A whistleblower talks to the press on air about healthy eating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Five a day' is the UK health advice to eat five portions of fruit and vegetables daily.
explanation.definitionFit: The vegetable counts toward the recommended five daily portions of produce.

clue.text: People get Euston's second fare list

parts.note: men means people

indicators.note: the second letter of the station's name is taken

explanation.surface: Travellers at Euston station look at the fares board.
explanation.walkthrough: Euston is a London rail terminus, which makes 'fare' look like a ticket price.
explanation.definitionFit: A restaurant's list of dishes, fare being food, is its bill of fare.

clue.text: Recorded terrible dirge without record player mostly

indicators.note: here without means outside, the rearranged dirge going round the other piece
a terrible dirge is badly played, so its letters are mangled
most but not all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a stereo is a record-playing system

explanation.surface: Someone taped a dreadful funeral song without using most of their hi-fi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here means outside, not lacking: the rearranged funeral song wraps round the shortened hi-fi.
explanation.definitionFit: Something registered has been entered officially in a record, so it is recorded.

clue.text: Inadvertently reveal the French doctor in Jersey perhaps

parts.note: le is French for the

indicators.note: the doctor goes inside the garment

parts.note: a jersey is a kind of top, a pullover

explanation.surface: A French doctor in Jersey lets slip a secret.
explanation.walkthrough: Jersey looks like the Channel Island, but it is a jumper.
explanation.definitionFit: To let something drop is to mention it casually, often without meaning to.

clue.text: Asian island's in good condition making use of traditional customs

indicators.note: the island's letters sit inside the other word

parts.note: in trim means in good shape
Bali is an Indonesian island; with the 's it gives BALIS

explanation.surface: An Asian island keeps its tidy look by upholding old ways.
explanation.definitionFit: Tribal loyalty and adherence to a group's ancestral ways are both described by this term.

clue.text: It will build body — heavenly one if given a start

indicators.note: the answer becomes the heavenly body when an A is put at its start

parts.note: an asteroid is a heavenly body

explanation.surface: A bodybuilding product is said to be out of this world once you get started.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer with A in front becomes ASTEROID.
explanation.definitionFit: Anabolic drugs of this type are taken to build muscle.

clue.text: Leaves chaps in revolt

indicators.note: the letters rise up and overturn their order

explanation.surface: The men walk out in a mutiny.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb about the men departing, but it is a noun: green leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: The vegetable is eaten as leaves, a leafy green.

clue.text: That man personally makes songs, little being articulated

indicators.note: articulated means spoken aloud, so the words are judged by their sound

parts.note: hymns are songs; an elf is a little being

explanation.surface: A man composes songs himself, his speech barely audible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little being' gives an elf, a tiny creature; 'articulated' is the signal that the words are spoken.
explanation.definitionFit: The reflexive pronoun is used to stress that a man does something personally.

clue.text: Old car journey hard without acceptable motorway

indicators.note: without means outside here, the journey and hard going round the rest

parts.note: a trip is a journey
U means upper-class, so socially acceptable
M designates a British motorway, as in the M1
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A tough trip in a vintage car, avoiding a decent motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' means outside, so TRIPH goes round UM. U is old British slang for upper class, hence acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: Triumph was a British car maker whose models are now classics.

clue.text: Walk wearily from wild parties

indicators.note: wild parties are unruly, so the letters run riot

explanation.surface: Someone drags their feet home after riotous parties.
explanation.definitionFit: To trudge or plod about tiredly is the meaning.

clue.text: I was in charge of country

parts.note: ran means managed or was in charge of

explanation.surface: A ruler boasts of having governed a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Islamic Republic in the Middle East is a country.

clue.text: TV award endlessly given to a work by Austen

indicators.note: endlessly means without its final letter

parts.note: an Emmy is an American television award

explanation.surface: A television prize goes to an adaptation of a Jane Austen book.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen's 1815 novel about a matchmaking heroine is titled with her name.

clue.text: Subject for photograph

parts.note: to can stand for for, as in a toast to someone
pic is short for picture or photograph

explanation.surface: Someone poses as a subject for a photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: A topic is a subject of discussion or writing.

clue.text: Bear father's letters?

definitions.meaning: a large black-and-white animal from China

explanation.walkthrough: The second reading spells out the letters of PA: P and A.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant panda is a bear native to China.

clue.text: Sweet enthusiast scoffing last of caramel

indicators.note: to scoff is to eat greedily, so the fan swallows the letter

parts.note: a fan is an enthusiast

indicators.note: only the final letter of the word is used

explanation.surface: A dessert lover wolfs down the end of the caramel.
explanation.definitionFit: A flan is a tart, often a sweet dessert; sweet is British for a pudding.

clue.text: Steaks, etc, make old king poorly

parts.note: GR is Georgius Rex, King George
poorly means ill

explanation.surface: Eating steaks makes an old monarch sick.
explanation.definitionFit: A mixed grill is a dish of grilled meats such as steaks, chops and sausages.

clue.text: Compose neat prose in synthetic language

indicators.note: composing puts the letters together in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A writer is told to produce tidy prose in an invented tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Esperanto is a constructed international language invented by Zamenhof.

clue.text: Austen's work is subject of study taken in by male and female novelist

parts.note: a man is a male

indicators.note: the study subject is absorbed inside the novelist's name

parts.note: Muriel Spark was a Scottish novelist
a field is an area or subject of study

explanation.surface: A novel by Austen is studied by both a man and a woman writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novelist' suggests Katherine Mansfield, but the woman writer is Muriel Spark, with FIELD inside her name.
explanation.definitionFit: Jane Austen wrote the 1814 novel about Fanny Price, so it is one of her works.
